title: Transcendent training review (from an hypertrophy standpoint)
summary: Reviews 'transcendent training' (taking a 20-rep weight up to a single 100-rep set, resting only while holding the weight). It works for hypertrophy as high-volume training and builds mental toughness, like widowmaker squats, but it suits only certain lifts, biases toward lower body, invites form breakdown, is below a useful intensity window, and is ultimately less work than a proper volume day.

claims.claim: Transcendent training means getting 100 reps on one exercise, either starting with a weight you can do 100 times and adding weight, or starting with a 20-rep weight and building to 100; he only reviews the second.
The first version is usually done daily in a Bulgarian/Wisconsin style, meaning lots of work outside any useful intensity window, which he considers not good for hypertrophy.
Widowmaker squats (a 12-rep weight taken to 30+ reps, resting at the top) work extremely well for hypertrophy, which lends credit to transcendent training.
These high-rep methods work on squats because standing with the bar isn't taxing for the quads and posterior chain, so you can recover at the top without racking.
Floor pulls don't suit the method because you can rest as long as you want with the bar on the floor, defeating the purpose; same for any lift where you set the weight down.
Grip limits many lifts; for 100-rep RDLs you'd need straps, and straps start cutting into the wrists and circulation beyond about 30-40 reps.
Jumping from 20 to 40 reps in one session reflects mental fortitude, not doubled strength, so you can't tell how much real strength or hypertrophy you're getting.
It works for hypertrophy because it is essentially high-volume training, and volume drives hypertrophy.
100 reps is basically a 10x10 with no rest; he believes being able to rest between sets would be better.
People new to high volume will be very sore for four or five days, maybe a week, and may struggle to train through it.
Form breaks down over 100 reps; with submaximal loads it isn't acutely injurious but grinding bad reps causes overuse injuries over time.
Like the Wisconsin method it creates a lower body bias, since high reps with heavy-ish weight are easier on legs, leaving the upper body (which needs more work to grow) neglected.
Bro training (chest and arms obsession) has been replaced by powerlifting bro training (posterior chain and legs obsession), which is just as unbalanced and awful for bodybuilding.
Upper body options are limited: bench needs spotters or safeties, and lockout on bench is not a resting position; cable work lets you rest between reps at will.
Claims that it reduces fat in the targeted area are unverified; he hasn't tried the system himself.
100 reps in one go is actually lazy: a proper volume day does far more than 100 reps and moves more total weight.
You can get the same mental-fortitude benefit from hard sets in the 8-12 rep range.
A weight you can do 100 times is not challenging; for natural hypertrophy stay within an intensity window where sets of 20-35 are the upper limit, or it becomes junk volume.
He does tons of volume and never goes very low reps, yet calls this method not intense enough, which should give people pause.
Don't use transcendent training as your first taste of high volume: you'll burn out, recovery may fail, and you might get sick.
It suits people who once had high work capacity and want to rebuild it quickly, done in cycles.
It isn't enough for hypertrophy on its own because it focuses on one body part at a time; a bodybuilding program must cover the whole body and rotate intensity and volume.
Using it to bring up a lagging body part is risky: lagging parts already respond well to any extra volume and isolation, so throwing everything at them can injure you or wreck recovery.
If you enjoy trying a new method, it's fine to do it for fun.
